bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
bullet_feedback.problem: The sentence ends on a trailing clause, 'and backtesting it', after a comma list ('like patching, balancing availability against cost'). On first read, 'balancing availability against cost' looks like a third item in the 'like patching' list, and 'it' could mean the logic or the bounds.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top bullet under the biggest brand on the page. A backend screener who has to re-read it to separate the example (patching) from the goal (availability vs cost) loses the one place the page shows big-tech production work.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Put the verbs together and end the 'like patching' example cleanly before giving the goal. For example: 'Writing and backtesting Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, to balance availability against cost'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
bullet_feedback.problem: This is the first Capital One bullet and it is the most frontend one in the role (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow), while the two backend bullets beneath it hold the role's stronger systems evidence.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Your question is whether the strongest backend and cloud evidence shows up first, and it doesn't here. A backend reader skimming the first line of each role sees a UI rebuild under Capital One and may label the internship as frontend before reaching the latency and caching work.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder within the role so the 65% generation-time bullet leads and this one comes last. The text can stay as it is.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows, so lookups rarely touch a database gated by permissions and rate limits
bullet_feedback.problem: 'a category tree that the Claude skill searches first' doesn't say what the tree is keyed on or what a lookup is. 'with Redis caching full workflows' is attached without a verb, so the bullet reads as two mechanisms joined by a comma.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most backend-shaped design on the page: precompute, cache, and avoid an expensive permissioned DB. A reader who can't picture the data flow (tree for routing, Redis for payloads, DB as fallback) will see buzzwords rather than a design.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the category tree is keyed on, and whether Redis is checked before or after the tree
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lay out the read path in order, with a verb for each step: tree to find the workflow, Redis to fetch it, database only on a miss. Don't add a hit rate unless one exists.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a research tool that scores and aggregates topics so Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff can see what’s popular, running in dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code ready for production
bullet_feedback.problem: The second half is a chain of four technologies ('AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code'), and the first half's 'scores and aggregates topics' doesn't say what is scored or from what data.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The honest 'running in dev ... ready for production' scoping is good. But the bullet reads more like a deployment stack than something you engineered, and the Skills section already lists all four technologies.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what a 'topic' is (e.g. extracted from the scraped documents) and what you specifically owned in the co-build
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the dev/production scoping and one deployment noun that shows ownership (e.g. the CDK infrastructure). Use the freed space to say what the tool scores topics from.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (total, per day, or per run), so the reader can't tell the pipeline's load.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Backend interviewers size a streaming design by throughput. Without a unit, the Kinesis choice could look like overkill for a one-time batch of 6,000 documents.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 6,000+ is a total corpus or a recurring volume
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the existing scope unit if one exists. Otherwise leave the bullet as it is, since the technique and result are clear.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
bullet_feedback.problem: The bullet ends on intent ('to reduce database load and latency') with no outcome. The 20,000+ visits number describes the product, not the caching work, so it reads as if it measures the change.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the second Redis caching bullet on the page and it is weaker than the Capital One one. A reader may read the visits figure as an impact claim, and one follow-up ('what did the cache change?') would expose the gap.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether any before/after load or latency was observed; if not, keep the wording as intent
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Make it clear that 20,000+ visits is the traffic the cache served, e.g. lead with the scheduler and its traffic, then the caching. Or say what the cache keys on so the bullet shows a decision rather than a goal.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest systems evidence on the page, the C++ order book with B+ tree vs LSM backends, sits at the bottom under Projects, below a robotics bullet and a student-studio role.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend or performance-minded interviewer sees thin AWS work and frontend-first Capital One work before reaching the bullets they would most want to ask about. Readers who stop at the middle of the page miss them.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider moving Projects above TerpLabs/UMIACS, or at least leading Capital One with its backend bullets, so the first third of the page shows the backend and performance story. Keep Experience brands at the top.

page_feedback.problem: Jargon that only AI-tooling readers know: 'Claude skill', 'sub-skills', 'AnyGrasp', 'vision-language model', 'RAG'. These appear without a gloss across three roles.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter or general backend screener can't restate the Capital One generation-time bullet without knowing what a 'skill' is, which weakens one of the page's best metrics.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Gloss 'Claude skill' once in plain words the first time it appears (e.g. 'the Claude-based workflow generator's'). Leave the rest.

page_feedback.problem: Skills section filler: 'data structures and algorithms', 'Agile', 'Jira' take space without informing a backend reader. Backend items (REST APIs, PostgreSQL, Redis) are mixed with React/Electron under 'Backend & Full-Stack'.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor. The section parses well for ATS, but the backend line is diluted.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Optionally drop the generic practice terms, or split frontend items onto their own line so the backend line reads as backend.
